newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia ups oil imports to counter shortages.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia ups oil imports to counter shortages.

text.p: Yugoslavia has revised upwards its 1997 import quotas for oil and oil derivatives to secure regular petrol supplies, a Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce and Industry official said on Monday.
"Import quotas for oil and oil products were increased last week to avoid possible market imbalances," the head of the Chamber's energy committee Buda Kotri told Reuters.
"We expect new quotas to ensure regular petrol supplies and to satisfy domestic needs by the year end," he said.

The government increased import quotas for petrol to 130,000 tonnes from 55,000 tonnes, diesel and heating oil to 160,000 tonnes from 100,000 tonnes and primary petrol to 300,000 tonnes from 150,000 tonnes.
In July many petrol stations throughout the country dried up and long queues reappeared at the few state-held pumps that are regularly supplied.
The officials said a significant increase in vehicles, summer holidays and the harvest were behind the swollen demand.
Lower supply was blamed on problems at the Pancevo oil refinery. During almost a month and a half long breakdown, petrol output fell to only 1,000 tonnes a day, insufficient to meet increased demand.
"Since the fault has been repaired, production has already reached 2,300 tonnes per day which completely satisfies the market needs," said Kotri.
But industry analysts blamed fuel shortages on the failure of the Yugoslav-Chinese oil barter deal and the monopoly state companies hold over imports.

Serbia's state company NIS Jugopetrol, subsidiary of Naftna Industrija Srbije (NIS), and China's Sinochem signed a 5-year barter deal in March last year under which two million tonnes of crude oil should have been imported from China in exchange for Yugoslav products.
"Imports of fuel in the first half of the year were well below plan as the NIS Jugopetrol barter deal fell through," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
"Our industries simply do not have sufficient domestic products to meet counter-delivery requirements. And anyhow, it is not a real barter arrangement as the Chinese have set world prices," he added.
Government statistics said Yugoslav January-June imports from China stood at $31 million and exports at only $5 million, resulting in a $26 million deficit.
Consumers have also used more fuel as Yugoslavia recovers from the 1992-1996 U.N trade embargo, imposed for backing Serb military action in neighbouring Bosnia.

The number of petrol stations has doubled in the past years, to 1,200. Some 400 are private and the rest belong to Serbia's NIS Jugopetrol (some 550), Beopetrol (200) and Montenegrin Jugopetrol-Kotor (50).
Yugoslavia's consumption of oil and oil products was expected to rise by 18 percent to 3.8 million tonnes this year. -- Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 311 4254
